title: Intel Diamond Rapids shows signs of life in SC26 demo running live server
summary: Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at two booths during SC26, one of which featured a running server, but neither were directly from Intel.
body: Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 ( SC26 ) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly. Most interesting was a running server at the CXL booth, showcasing a demo with a Diamond Rapids CPU. The server ran for the first day of the show, and upon returning to the booth, we were informed that it had been shut down due to noise complaints (it’s hard to mistake a running server). Elsewhere at Bull’s booth, a Diamond Rapids CPU was shown installed in a server behind a glass case. Notably, Intel didn’t have a Diamond Rapids demo, instead focusing most of its booth on Xeon 6+ and its new D270 GPU, otherwise known as Crescent Island . The demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller. If you’re unfamiliar, memory expansion via CXL is an increasingly common tactic to give multi-host environments access to a large pool of memory, breaking free of an individual server’s capacity via CXL. In the demo, Montage is showing off its memory expansion controller running across a Xeon 6 and a Diamond Rapids server, each sharing a pool of memory over CXL. title: Nvidia GeForce driver bug reportedly hammers SSDs with up to 30GB of writes per hour
summary: Nvidia’s GeForce 621.14 and 621.24 drivers reportedly rewrite a log file nonstop, writing gigabytes to SSDs every hour.
body: Nvidia’s GeForce driver 621.14 is reportedly causing excessive background writes on idle PCs, inducing extra wear on SSDs. One user measured about 3GB an hour on the susceptible driver, and another mentioned estimated up to 30GB/hour on the newer 621.24. This follows a similar-looking bug from AMD’s video driver discovered last month. The bug is described by user Andergraude in an Nvidia forum post as “new in 621.14,” which came out on Nov. 4, who says it operates by “continuously [rewriting] the binary log file” with “real writes” to the drive. The writes are coming from the NVDisplay.Container.exe process, or the “NVIDIA Display Container LS” service, which logs to the nvlog.nvlgstg file. This background service is necessary for running the Nvidia Control Panel and App. It’s not clear what’s written in the log, and not every system is necessarily impacted. The “real writes” point comes from the fact that a per-process write counter is not the same as writes reaching the drive. The measurements came from Windows Resource Monitor, Windows performance counters, and CrystalDiskInfo. The Data Units Written counter matched Windows’ reporting. This test showed 515MB of process I/O comi…

title: GTA VI runs at 1440p on PS5 and Xbox Series X, but just 720p with upscaling on Series S

body: The most highly anticipated video game of the decade is here. GTA VI arrives almost 13 years after GTA V , with reports suggesting that it has already generated around $1.54 billion in revenue from 16 million preorders. Ahead of its release, Rockstar Games has finally shared some technical details, including rendering resolutions and upscaling technologies being used across all consoles. In a statement shared with Wccftech , the technical team at Rockstar has confirmed that GTA VI uses different upscaling solutions across all consoles in order to achieve a balance between visual quality and performance with a target of 30FPS. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use Rockstar's own temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) solution, while the PlayStation 5 Pro relies on Sony's second-generation PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR2). The Xbox Series S, meanwhile, relies on AMD's FSR 4 upscaling technology. As for rendered resolutions, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and PlayStation 5 Pro all start with a native base resolution of 1440p, which is then upscaled to 4K. While the market's rapid growth is impressive regardless, there are good reasons why OLED monitors are becoming increasingly popular: they're getting cheaper, better, and considerably easier to justify . ASUS maintained its position as the world's largest OLED monitor vendor, accounting for 21.7% of shipments. MSI climbed into second place for the first time, capturing 14.5% of the market, while Samsung slipped to third with 11.3%. Both Taiwanese vendors have been particularly aggressive in the gaming monitor market, where increasingly competitive pricing has helped make OLED technology accessible to more buyers, while ubiquitous advertising with tech-conscious gamers has made them highly visible. title: SSDs, laptops, and phones may get cheaper as consumer NAND spot pricing drops 20%
summary: According to a new report, slowing demand for consumer electronics and diverging production requirements for consumer and enterprise NAND have resulted in declining spot prices for consumer-grade flash memory. Those trends may result in unexpected but welcome relief for consumers.
body: Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a new report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED). The report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction. SED says that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far." title: Budget-friendly gifts for gamers — keyboards, mice, headsets, and more under $80
summary: The best budget-friendly gifts for gamers — keyboards, mice, headsets, and more, all for under $80.
body: The gamers in your life might be hoping for a $7,000 graphics card (I know I am), but that doesn't mean they won't still appreciate some solid, significantly cheaper gaming peripherals. While $80 doesn't go quite as far as it used to, there are still plenty of awesome accessories that any gamer would be thrilled to receive — including headsets, mice, keyboards, microphones, mouse pads, and even an Elgato Stream Deck. Budget-friendly doesn't mean compromising on quality or convenience, either. While you won't be able to find all the bells and whistles at the sub-$80 level, there are both wired and wireless headsets, mice, and keyboards at this price point, including some last-generation flagship products. Razer's DeathAdder V3 Pro is currently on sale for $64.99 , and remains one of the best-feeling mice we've ever tested — and its shape was so good that Razer kept it, exactly, in the newer DeathAdder V4 Pro . HyperX's Cloud III gaming headset is basically identical to our favorite Cloud III S headset — the only real difference is that the Cloud III is wired, while the Cloud III S is wireless.
